title: Thyroid nodule and differentiated thyroid cancer
summary: Work up a thyroid nodule, tell papillary from follicular cancer, and manage and follow up DTC the way exams and current practice expect.
closing: Test first with TSH and ultrasound, let FNAC and histology each do only what they can, treat by risk, and follow with thyroglobulin.

objectives.text: Choose the first investigation for a solitary thyroid nodule, and say when a scan is needed and which test answers 'what is the nodule'
Tell how papillary carcinoma is diagnosed (nuclear features) from how follicular carcinoma is diagnosed (invasion on histology), and say what FNAC or frozen section can and cannot settle
Pick the thyroid cancer that is most common overall, in children, after radiation, in a thyroglossal cyst and in iodine deficiency, and name its commonest mutation
Tell the usual route and sites of spread of papillary versus follicular carcinoma, and exclude medullary and anaplastic from DTC
Choose the action for each Bethesda category, separating II from IV and V
Choose the extent of surgery for a given DTC (lobectomy versus total thyroidectomy), giving both the classic key and current practice
Decide who needs radioiodine, how TSH is raised before ablation, and how long-term TSH suppression is matched to risk
Pick the follow-up marker for DTC versus medullary carcinoma, and interpret thyroglobulin with antibodies and a negative radioiodine scan
Identify the commonest complication after thyroidectomy, match voice and airway changes to the nerve injured, and choose the first step for a neck haematoma
State the AJCC staging age cut-off and place the look-alikes (oncocytic, microcarcinoma, prognosis) correctly

traps.trap: FNAC is the first investigation for a solitary thyroid nodule (merges TR2: radionuclide scan first)
Follicular carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer
Cytology or frozen section can diagnose follicular carcinoma
Papillary carcinoma is diagnosed by its papillary architecture (merges TR9: psammoma bodies are PTC-exclusive)
An encapsulated follicular variant of PTC is a carcinoma
The AJCC age cut-off for DTC staging is 45 years
Total thyroidectomy is the treatment for all differentiated thyroid cancer (merges TR19: one size cut-off)
A lateral aberrant thyroid is ectopic thyroid tissue
Papillary spreads by blood and follicular spreads by lymphatics
Cervical lymph nodes are the usual site of follicular carcinoma spread (merges TR13: medullary and anaplastic counted as DTC)
A negative radioiodine scan rules out recurrence when thyroglobulin is raised
Radioiodine is given to every DTC patient
Bethesda II nodule needs surgery
Bethesda IV and V mean the same management
Loss of high-pitched voice is recurrent laryngeal nerve injury
The most common complication after thyroidectomy is nerve injury or bleeding
A neck haematoma is first managed by reintubation
TSH should be suppressed before radioiodine ablation (merges TR17: one TSH target for every risk group)
A low thyroglobulin is reassuring when anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are present
Calcitonin is the marker for differentiated thyroid cancer

segments.title: The nodule in the clinic: first test or test of choice?
segments.goal: Let the learner fail the old 'FNAC first' key, then separate first investigation from investigation of choice.

segments.title: Papillary versus follicular: how each is diagnosed
segments.goal: Contrast nuclear diagnosis of papillary with invasion-based diagnosis of follicular, and the most-common labels.

prefer.reason: Paired contrasting cases fit papillary-versus-follicular and the which-is-NOT multi-trap close

segments.title: Where does it spread? Lymph or blood
segments.goal: Reverse the spread routes, list follicular sites, and place medullary and anaplastic outside DTC.

segments.title: From Bethesda to the operating table
segments.goal: Map Bethesda categories to actions and pick the extent of surgery by size and risk.

prefer.reason: Management segments won with per-step probes in two forms and a fast lane

segments.title: Radioiodine and TSH: who, how, and why
segments.goal: Reason why radioiodine needs high TSH while later suppression needs low TSH, and who gets ablation.

prefer.reason: Causal ladder: iodine uptake needs TSH drive, so predict-then-show

segments.title: Follow-up: markers, antibodies and the negative scan
segments.goal: Climb the ladder calcitonin versus thyroglobulin, antibodies, negative scan with raised Tg, plus the staging age.

prefer.reason: Faded worked example for follow-up ladder; Tg interpretation is a stepwise algorithm

segments.title: After the operation: complications
segments.goal: Match the commonest complication, voice versus airway change and the first step for a haematoma.
